title.analysis: Authentic title "How Inflation Quietly Stole Your Raise" uses an explanatory "how" frame with a theft metaphor and second-person address. The script delivers it via cumulative-inflation arithmetic and a $50,000 raise example. It is a calm, low-novelty title relative to the cohort's STRONG peers, which lean on wealth thresholds and secrecy ("When You Get Rich, Tell NO ONE!", "Why Everything Changes After You Hit $1,000,000 Invested") or specific traps ("The Car Payment Trap Nobody Talks About"). This video is WEAK against that cohort; association only, no CTR or experiment evidence.

script.opening_words: You just got that raise you've been waiting for, and for about 5 minutes, you felt like you'd finally made it. Maybe you celebrated with a nice dinner out, or perhaps you started mentally spending that extra money on things you've been putting off, but then reality hits you like a freight train carrying a cargo full of grocery bills. Somehow, despite earning more money than ever before, your bank account still feels like it's running on fumes, and you're
script.ending_words: is like putting a band-aid on a broken leg. Like it The economy has fundamentally changed the rules while you were busy being a responsible adult. But now, you know what's really happening, and knowledge is power. Start protecting your purchasing power today through smart investing, ruthless expense cutting, and strategic income increases. Your future self will thank you for taking action instead of just hoping things magically get better.
script.analysis: Full 18573 canonical characters read. A cumulative-inflation explainer: hook (raise feels gone), headline CPI and cumulative price rise since February 2020, nominal vs real wages, salary budgets, housing/property tax/utilities, food and eggs, gasoline, Yale tariff estimate, a $50,000 raise example, a median-earner budget breakdown, household spending and card debt, then defensive tools (savings vs inflation, TIPS, I bonds), offensive hedges (real estate, stocks, commodities), expense cutting (subscriptions, transport, housing) and a close. Verified: 3.0% CPI to September 2025, gasoline +4.1% (largest monthly factor), I-bond 1.10%/2.86%/3.98%. Understated: cumulative price rise is about 25.6%, not 23%. Stale: Conference Board 3.9% (a 2024 projection; actual 2025 was 3.4%), $5,577/month spending (2021 CE), February 2025 food figures mixed with September 2025 data. Arithmetic: the raise example and interest examples reproduce; the budget total is off by $500-800 and the residual per month is $1,383, not ~$1,300. The real-wage figures (3.9%/1.5%) are inconsistent with 2025 CPI. The script contradicts itself on transport ($500 vs $900/month). The real-estate hedge passage is partly lost to an ASR splice. The stored ending is complete.
beat_map: Cold open: the raise disappears into grocery bills.
Headline CPI 3% and cumulative 23% since Feb 2020.
Nominal 3.9% vs real 1.5% wages; cumulative-gap analogy; Conference Board 3.9% budgets.
Housing: $437K median, mortgage rates, $117K income; property taxes; utilities.
Month-to-month vs cumulative framing; Yale Budget Lab $2,500.
Turn to action: savings lose 2% real; TIPS; I bonds 3.98%.
Offensive hedges: real estate (partly lost), pricing-power stocks, commodities, diversification.
Close: protect purchasing power via investing, cutting and income.

topic.analysis: Cumulative inflation since 2020 outpacing nominal raises, with consumer-level arithmetic and generic inflation-hedge and expense-cutting advice.
topic.audience_problem: Workers who received raises but feel no better off and blame their own budgeting.
topic.time_sensitivity: Medium-high: specific CPI, I-bond and tariff figures date within months.
topic.narrative_angle: Your raise was a pay cut in disguise; here is the math and the defences.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Test an original raise-vs-inflation video built on one dated, reproducible table (CPI-U ratio, wage series, I-bond formula) with an interactive "your raise" calculation, keeping all figures to one reference month instead of mixing February and September data.
topic.competition: Same-channel nearest-age peers in K01; not an independent niche or causal test

virality.analysis: Frozen 6099 views / 300.5615 days = 20.29202 views/day. Against 10 peers 0.12069x (WEAK); against 5 peers 0.23410x (WEAK). Clearly below the cohort median (WEAK). The cohort contains several STRONG wealth-threshold and trap titles; this generic cost-of-living explainer underperformed them, consistent with (not proof of) lower novelty. Comment rate is computed in observed_result; whether audiences were saturated with inflation content in late 2025 is unmeasured.
